questions.stem: A data set has $n$ items. The sum of the items is $800$ and the mean is $20$.

parts.label: b
parts.intro: The standard deviation of this data set is $3$. Each value in the set is multiplied by $10$.
parts.text:
(i) Write down the value of the new mean.

(ii) Find the value of the new variance.
parts.markscheme:
(i) $200$ ***A1*** ***N1***

(ii) **METHOD 1**

recognizing variance $= \sigma^2$ ***(M1)***

eg $3^2 = 9$

correct working to find new variance ***(A1)***

eg $\sigma^2 \times 10^2$, $9 \times 100$

$900$ ***A1*** ***N3***

**METHOD 2**

new standard deviation is $30$ ***(A1)***

recognizing variance $= \sigma^2$ ***(M1)***

eg $3^2 = 9$, $30^2$

$900$ ***A1*** ***N3***

questions.stem:
The following diagram shows a circle with centre O and radius $r\text{ cm}$.

**diagram not to scale**

![Circle with centre O and radius r; the shaded sector AOB has angle θ at O.](content/papers/img/2018-may-p1-tz2-q4.png)

The points A and B lie on the circumference of the circle, and $\text{A}\hat{\text{O}}\text{B} = \theta$. The area of the shaded sector AOB is $12\text{ cm}^2$ and the length of arc AB is $6\text{ cm}$.

parts.markscheme:
evidence of correctly substituting into circle formula (may be seen later) ***A1A1***

eg $\dfrac{1}{2}\theta r^2 = 12$, $r\theta = 6$

attempt to eliminate one variable ***(M1)***

eg $r = \dfrac{6}{\theta}$, $\theta = \dfrac{l}{r}$, $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\theta r^2}{r\theta} = \dfrac{12}{6}$

correct elimination ***(A1)***

eg $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{r} \times r^2 = 12$, $\dfrac{1}{2}\theta \times \left(\dfrac{6}{\theta}\right)^2 = 12$, $A = \dfrac{1}{2} \times r^2 \times \dfrac{l}{r}$, $\dfrac{r^2}{2r} = 2$

correct equation ***(A1)***

eg $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 6r = 12$, $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{36}{\theta} = 12$, $12 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times r^2 \times \dfrac{6}{r}$

correct working ***(A1)***

eg $3r = 12$, $\dfrac{18}{\theta} = 12$, $\dfrac{r}{2} = 2$, $24 = 6r$

$r = 4$ (cm) ***A1*** ***N2***

questions.stem:
The following diagram shows the graph of a function $f$, for $-4 \leq x \leq 2$.

![Graph of f on a grid: a straight segment from (−4, 1) to (0, 0) and another from (0, 0) to (2, 2).](content/papers/img/2018-may-p1-tz2-q5-f.png)

parts.label: a
parts.text: On the same axes, sketch the graph of $f(-x)$.
parts.markscheme:
![The graph of f (grey) and its reflection f(−x) (black): segments from (−2, 2) to (0, 0) and from (0, 0) to (4, 1).](content/papers/img/2018-may-p1-tz2-q5a-ms.png)

***A2*** ***N2***

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Another function, $g$, can be written in the form $g(x) = a \times f(x + b)$. The following diagram shows the graph of $g$.

![Graph of g: a straight segment from (−3, −2) to (1, 0) and another from (1, 0) to (3, −4).](content/papers/img/2018-may-p1-tz2-q5-g.png)

Write down the value of $a$ and of $b$.
parts.markscheme:
recognizing horizontal shift/translation of $1$ unit ***(M1)***

eg $b = 1$, moved $1$ right

recognizing vertical stretch/dilation with scale factor $2$ ***(M1)***

eg $a = 2$, $y \times (-2)$

$a = -2$, $b = -1$ ***A1A1*** ***N2N2***

parts.text: Let $f(x) = px^2 + qx - 4p$, where $p \neq 0$. Find the number of roots for the equation $f(x) = 0$. Justify your answer.
parts.markscheme:
**METHOD 1**

evidence of discriminant ***(M1)***

eg $b^2 - 4ac$, $\Delta$

correct substitution into discriminant ***(A1)***

eg $q^2 - 4p(-4p)$

correct discriminant ***A1***

eg $q^2 + 16p^2$

$16p^2 > 0$ (accept $p^2 > 0$) ***A1***

$q^2 \geq 0$ (do not accept $q^2 > 0$) ***A1***

$q^2 + 16p^2 > 0$ ***A1***

$f$ has 2 roots ***A1*** ***N0***

**METHOD 2**

$y$-intercept $= -4p$ (seen anywhere) ***A1***

if $p$ is positive, then the $y$-intercept will be negative ***A1***

an upward-opening parabola with a negative $y$-intercept ***R1***

eg sketch that must indicate $p > 0$.

if $p$ is negative, then the $y$-intercept will be positive ***A1***

a downward-opening parabola with a positive $y$-intercept ***R1***

eg sketch that must indicate $p < 0$.

$f$ has 2 roots ***A2*** ***N0***

questions.stem:
A closed cylindrical can with radius $r$ centimetres and height $h$ centimetres has a volume of $20\pi\text{ cm}^3$.

**diagram not to scale**

![A closed cylinder with radius r and height h.](content/papers/img/2018-may-p1-tz2-q9.png)

parts.label: a
parts.markscheme:
correct equation for volume ***(A1)***

eg $\pi r^2 h = 20\pi$

$h = \dfrac{20}{r^2}$ ***A1*** ***N2***

parts.label: b
parts.intro: The material for the base and top of the can costs $10$ cents per $\text{cm}^2$ and the material for the curved side costs $8$ cents per $\text{cm}^2$. The total cost of the material, in cents, is $C$.
parts.markscheme:
attempt to find formula for cost of parts ***(M1)***

eg $10 \times$ two circles, $8 \times$ curved side

correct expression for cost of two circles in terms of $r$ (seen anywhere) ***A1***

eg $2\pi r^2 \times 10$

correct expression for cost of curved side (seen anywhere) ***(A1)***

eg $2\pi r \times h \times 8$

correct expression for cost of curved side in terms of $r$ ***A1***

eg $8 \times 2\pi r \times \dfrac{20}{r^2}$, $\dfrac{320\pi r}{r^2}$

$C = 20\pi r^2 + \dfrac{320\pi}{r}$ ***AG*** ***N0***

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that there is a minimum value for $C$, find this minimum value in terms of $\pi$.
parts.markscheme:
recognize $C' = 0$ at minimum ***(R1)***

eg $C' = 0$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}r} = 0$

correct differentiation (may be seen in equation)

$C' = 40\pi r - \dfrac{320\pi}{r^2}$ ***A1A1***

correct equation ***A1***

eg $40\pi r - \dfrac{320\pi}{r^2} = 0$, $40\pi r = \dfrac{320\pi}{r^2}$

correct working ***(A1)***

eg $40r^3 = 320$, $r^3 = 8$

$r = 2$ (m) ***A1***

attempt to substitute **their** value of $r$ into $C$ ***(M1)***

eg $20\pi \times 4 + 320 \times \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

correct working ***(A1)***

eg $80\pi + 160\pi$

$240\pi$ (cents) ***A1*** ***N3***

> **Note:** Do not accept $753.6$, $753.98$ or $754$, even if $240\pi$ is seen.
